headline: SW Ledge Slack at 10:20: Bass to 34 Pounds, First Bonito Flash Off Sandy Point
subhead: A short tide window on the Ledge produced the best bass of the summer, while the first bonito show off Block Island and fluke stay a grind.
body_markdown:
Ten-twenty. That's the number I circled this week — the top of the tide at SW Ledge, when the current goes soft for about fifteen minutes before it turns and starts running back out toward Block Island Sound. Everybody who fishes that piece of water knows the real bite isn't at dead slack, it's in the ten minutes on either side of it, when the rip is still moving enough to hold bait against the ledge but not so hard you can't hold bottom in 40 feet. That's where we found a 34-pound bass Thursday morning, eel-hooked on a live eel drifted right down the edge where the sand drops into the rocks. Not a fluke catch — three boats out of Galilee reported fish over 30 pounds off the Ledge this week, all within an hour of that same tide stage.

The pattern makes sense once you look at the water. Kings Point up in the Sound is sitting at 71.2°F, New London back at 66.4°, and that west-to-east gradient is exactly why the bigger bass are staging where they are — pushing bait east and south out of the warmer Sound water and stacking it against structure like SW Ledge and the rips off North Light, where the temperature break itself creates a wall these fish use to pin forage. Montauk's reading 70.2, so there's a real corridor of comfortable water running from western Long Island Sound straight through our zone right now, and the bass are using it as a highway.

Tactically, if you're working the Ledge, I'm still leaning on eels after dark and at the tide changes, but daytime we've had better luck bouncing 2-ounce bucktails tipped with a chunk of squid strip along the bottom in 35 to 45 feet, working the drift from the sea buoy down toward the rockpile. Slow retrieve, let it hit bottom every third or fourth crank. The fish aren't chasing hard right now — they're eating stuff that looks like it's already dying, which tracks with what the bluefish blitzes have been doing to the peanut bunker pods working through there.

Speaking of bluefish — East End reports have jumbo classes mixing into the same current edges as the bass, and we're seeing that here too. If you get into a boil off Sandy Point, don't automatically assume bass. I've had guys hook up on what they swore was a 40-inch striper and boat an 14-pound blue instead. Both are eating in the same water column right now because the bait doesn't care what's chasing it.

Fluke has been the tougher story. We're picking through a lot of shorts on the south side of the Block, working the drift from Southwest Point down toward the Ledge in 30 to 50 feet with white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, tipped with squid. The keeper grade is there but it's not thick — for every 19-inch fish we're culling four or five shorts. Best window has been the first two hours of the outgoing, when the current's got enough push to keep your bait moving but hasn't ripped so hard you're dragging bottom sideways. Coxs Ledge has fished a little better for size if you want to make the run — a few boats came back with fluke pushing 6 pounds out there this week, but that's a 45-minute run each way from Galilee and the swell out of the south has made that ride uncomfortable more days than not.

Which brings me to sea state — buoy readings offshore have been holding around 2.3 feet at a 10-second period out of the southeast, which isn't rough, but it's enough of a rolling groundswell that anything east of the Ledge has been a bit of a washing machine on the smaller boats. If you're running a center console under 24 feet, I'd keep your Block Island days to mornings before that swell builds with the afternoon sea breeze.

Now the fun one — bonito. We had our first flashes off Sandy Point and down toward Southeast Light this week, small pods showing on the surface chasing sand eels in that clean, cobalt water south of the Block. Nobody's boxed one yet that I've heard of firsthand, but the guys trolling small Deadly Dicks and green machines behind the boat on wire have had shots at them. This is right on schedule — mid-July is when they typically start showing off the island, about two to three weeks ahead of when they'll actually commit to biting with any consistency. I wouldn't build a whole trip around bonito yet, but if you're already out there working bass or fluke, it's worth keeping a light spinning rod rigged with a small metal on deck just in case you run into surface activity.

Black sea bass have stayed steady and honestly less dramatic than everything else — square-tail jigs and clam-baited hi-lo rigs over the rockpiles east of the Ledge and around the Southwest side of Block Island are still producing a good grade, plenty of fish in the 16 to 18-inch range mixed with shorts, dependable if unspectacular.

Looking ahead: if that thermal gradient holds — warm water pushing from the Sound side, cooler water still sitting to our east — I expect the bass bite at SW Ledge to stay tied to that tide window around the top of the flood and the first hour of the ebb. That's where I'd spend my time this weekend. The bonito window will widen as the water stabilizes through late July, so keep that metal rigged. Fluke I'd call a grind until we get a real push of bigger fish through — worth doing, just don't expect it easy.
